學習英國管通常由雙簧管演奏者兼任，操作順序為將雙簧片直接裝入彎曲金屬管，再接上管: The English horn is usually learnt by oboe players as a second instrument. The order of assembly is to fit the double reed directly into the curved metal crook and then join that to the body. It sounds on the same principle as the oboe, by the vibration of the reed; the reed is wider and longer, with its two blades held at the base by metal wire, which steadies the timbre and the pitch. A beginner's focus is the oboe fingering, control of the reed's vibration, and the fact that a written note sounds a perfect fifth below.

約1720年西里西亞，Weigel家族將球狀喇叭口加於oboe da cacci: Around 1720 in Silesia the Weigel family added a bulbous bell to the curved body of the oboe da caccia type, forming the prototype of the modern English horn. The name does not come from England; because the early form looked like the horn blown by angels in medieval religious images, German-speaking areas called it engellisches Horn, which became English horn. From 1749 corno inglese appears in Italian, German and Austrian scores, and the earliest specific orchestral part is in Jommelli's opera Ezio; Gluck and Haydn used it in the 1750s, and the first concertos appeared in the 1770s. After the nineteenth century it drew more attention through works by Bellini, Rossini and Berlioz, but it was not much used in France before 1800 or in Britain before the 1830s.

In 1771 the Schwarzenberg wind band used two English horns alongside oboe, bassoon and horn; early on it also appeared in oboe trios. The English horn is a double-reed woodwind of the oboe family, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112-71. Its body is about one and a half times the oboe's length, it is a transposing instrument in F, and its fingering and blowing are close to the oboe's, so it is usually taken up by oboe players. A slightly curved metal crook joins the double reed, the bell is pear-shaped, and the timbre is deeper and softer than the oboe's. It is common in orchestras, opera and chamber music, used for a darker, pastoral or dreamlike colour; some works also write solo or concerto passages for it.

The sounding reed is made of cane folded into two blades, wider and longer than an oboe reed, usually with a metal wire at the base that holds the blades and steadies the timbre and pitch.
